clue.text: Inadequate type crazy about ancient virtues

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word for crazy is read backwards

parts.note: crazy means mad
ancient means aged
virtues are goods, good qualities

explanation.surface: Someone fanatically devoted to old-fashioned morals is dismissed as a feeble specimen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the reversal signal here, not a containment; 'virtues' are goods in the old sense of good qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically, a person seen as flawed or second-rate is called damaged goods.

clue.text: Removes weaknesses from schemes?

parts.note: the prefix de- signals removal, as in de-ice or defrost
vices are moral weaknesses

explanation.surface: A question whether clever plans can take the flaws out of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as DE-VICES, the answer would mean taking away vices; the question mark flags that playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: Devices are plans or stratagems, as in left to one's own devices.

clue.text: Claudius's offence, knocking over drink, spoiled restful mood

indicators.note: knocking over a glass upends it, so the drink's name is read backwards

parts.note: rum is a drink

indicators.note: spoiled signals that the following letters are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A villain's crime ruins a calm atmosphere by upsetting a glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking over' turns RUM into MUR; 'spoiled' rearranges RESTFUL MOOD into DERMOSTFOUL.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from Hamlet, where the Ghost describes the killing committed by his brother Claudius in these words.

clue.text: Energy that's short in German town

parts.note: go means energy or vigour

indicators.note: short means the word loses its final letter, cut off at the end

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a German town is lacking in vitality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims the final letter; the 's of that's is just 'is', joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Gotha is a town in Thuringia, central Germany, known for its almanac and ducal house.

clue.text: One has nothing in City (London?), or ridiculously little

indicators.note: in places the run of letters for one-has-nothing inside the city name

parts.note: Derry is the city also called Londonderry, so it is the city that may have London in front
one is the Roman numeral I
has is shortened to 's, giving S
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A remark on someone in a city with nothing, and an amount laughably small.
explanation.walkthrough: DERRY is a city in Northern Ireland, called Londonderry by some; the question mark marks the London prefix as optional. 'in' puts ISO inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A derisory sum is so small as to invite scorn, laughably inadequate.

clue.text: Bloody good to drop in to this party

indicators.note: to drop in suggests the letter for good falls from the front further into the word

parts.note: bloody means gory

explanation.surface: A guest is told to pop into a rather wild celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to drop in' moves the G of GORY from the front to third place. 'this' just points to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy is a wild party of unrestrained indulgence.

clue.text: Very severe damage rain can do

indicators.note: damage signals the letters that follow are smashed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A remark about how terrible the harm from heavy rain can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damage' rearranges RAINCANDO into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Draconian laws are excessively harsh, after Draco the strict Athenian lawgiver.

clue.text: How determinedly one sinks a bad pint?

definitions.text: How determinedly one sinks a bad pint?

parts.words: How determinedly one sinks a bad pint?
parts.note: the phrase for persisting to the finish read literally: downing a pint of beer of the bitter variety right to its final drop

explanation.surface: A drinker resolutely finishes a nasty glass of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British style of beer; the phrase means persisting to the very end, whatever the cost.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means resolutely continuing to the very last, however hard it becomes.

clue.text: Scientist's just invented a unit of weight

parts.note: something just invented is new
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A scientist has come up with a new measure of weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition includes the 's, read as 'Scientist is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton was the English physicist who described gravity; his name is also a unit of force.

clue.text: Appropriately clothed, run over a kilometre through Moscow

indicators.note: clothed means wrapped in a garment, so the garment's letters go round the letter for run

parts.note: a vest is the appropriate garment for a runner, so appropriately clothing a run means putting it in a vest
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A runner, properly dressed, covers just over a kilometre in the Russian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriately clothed' suggests the vest a runner wears; R goes inside VEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A verst is an old Russian measure of distance of about 1.07 kilometres.

clue.text: Complicated procedure to set up master part

parts.note: to rig is to set up, as with equipment
MA is a Master of Arts
a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: Instructions for preparing a lead part in a play turn out to be long-winded.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigmarole is a lengthy, tiresome process with many steps.

clue.text: Crack from vicar as sermon's starting in church

indicators.note: in puts the vicar-as-sermon letters inside the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a vicar is addressed as Rev, short for Reverend
taken as written

indicators.note: starting means the first letter of the following word is taken

explanation.surface: A rift opens as the vicar starts preaching in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' takes the first letter of sermon's, and 'in' puts the run inside CE, the Church of England; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A crevasse is a deep crack in a glacier or ice sheet.

clue.text: Decline to accept revolutionary surplice

indicators.note: to accept means the first word takes the second into itself

parts.note: rot is decay or decline
Che Guevara is the crossword's stock revolutionary

explanation.surface: A churchman refuses to put on a vestment of a radical design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to accept' signals containment; Che Guevara is the stock revolutionary in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A rochet is a white linen vestment like a surplice, worn by bishops.

clue.text: One sported in sun, getting dark red — ominous, at first

parts.note: sombre means dark in colour

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of each of the two words that come before it

explanation.surface: Someone out in the sunshine turns a gloomy red, a bad sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' takes R and O from red and ominous, after SOMBRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sombrero is a broad-brimmed hat worn for shade from the sun.

clue.text: Ruddy pig beginning to eat old coat

parts.note: ruddy means red
a pig is an oblong cast ingot of metal, as in pig iron

indicators.note: beginning to takes only the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A red-faced pig begins devouring an old jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes E from eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A redingote is a long double-breasted coat of the 18th century, its name from English riding coat.

clue.text: Animal turning head on rock

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the turned piece follows the rock

parts.note: Gib is short for Gibraltar, known as the Rock

indicators.note: turning means the word for head is read backwards

parts.note: nob is slang for head

explanation.surface: A creature turns its head while perched on a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' makes NOB into BON, which goes 'on' GIB.
explanation.definitionFit: A gibbon is a small long-armed ape of Southeast Asia.

clue.text: Sounded thick in opening of debate

parts.note: fat means thick
being in means being at home

indicators.note: opening of takes the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone spoke stupidly at the start of an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is HOME, as in 'stay in'; 'opening of' gives D from debate. 'Sounded' means measured depth, not spoke.
explanation.definitionFit: To sound water is to measure its depth, which is to fathom it.

clue.text: Doctor's manner when one died, carried out: very angry with himself

indicators.note: carried out means removed from the word, as a body is carried out

parts.note: a doctor's way with patients is the bedside manner

explanation.surface: A doctor fumes when a patient dies and is carried off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carried out' takes the D from BEDSIDE. The definition rests on 'beside himself' meaning frantic with anger; 'when one' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be beside oneself is to be overwhelmed by fury or emotion, so the word stands for that state.

clue.text: By speaking to engineers, one makes progress with two tiers

definitions.text: one makes progress with two tiers

indicators.note: speaking means the word is taken as it sounds, not as spelt

parts.note: the word by, said aloud, sounds like the prefix bi- meaning two
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: Someone talks with the engineers about advancing a two-storey project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. The definition describes an oared galley moving forward with two banks of rowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A bireme was an ancient galley propelled by two banks of oars, one above the other.

clue.text: Drawing me acting in play

indicators.note: in play signals the letters are in motion, being rearranged

explanation.surface: A sketch shows me performing in a theatre production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in play' rearranges MEACTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetic means attracting or drawing iron, and figuratively drawing people in.

clue.text: Fall of rebel, after money's short

indicators.note: after puts the rebel's name behind the shortened money
short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: cash is money
Jack Cade led a rebellion in Kent in 1450

explanation.surface: A revolutionary's downfall comes once his funds run low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims the final letter and 'after' puts the rebel second; Jack Cade led the 1450 Kentish revolt. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cascade is a waterfall, a fall of water over rocks.

clue.text: Taking pleasure in wine, unlikely to demand this?

indicators.note: taking means the wine word takes in the pleasure word

parts.note: red is wine
fun is pleasure

explanation.surface: A drinker enjoying a glass is hardly going to ask for money back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking' has RED take in FUN; 'in' is a link. A happy wine drinker would not ask for a repayment.
explanation.definitionFit: A refund is money paid back, which a satisfied customer would not ask for.

clue.text: Quality assurance personnel for American game

definitions.meaning: people who inspect products for faults
the US name for the board game draughts

explanation.definitionFit: Inspectors check things, and checkers is the American name for draughts.

clue.text: As strong-jawed type, one blooms

parts.note: a croc, short for crocodile, has powerful jaws
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A tough-jawed character blossoms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Croci is a plural of crocus, the spring-flowering bulb, so its flowers are blooms.

clue.text: Emperor's refusal to welcome queen

indicators.note: to welcome means the first word takes the second inside

parts.note: no is a refusal
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A ruler declines to receive a royal visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition includes the 's, read as 'Emperor is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was the Roman emperor of the first century AD.

clue.text: One may lie impressively in this memo — usual nonsense

definitions.text: One may lie impressively in this

indicators.note: nonsense signals the letters before it are turned into a jumble

explanation.surface: A note full of the familiar tosh might contain grand lies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nonsense' rearranges MEMOUSUAL. 'lie' means rest in death, not tell a fib.
explanation.definitionFit: A mausoleum is a grand tomb in which a body lies in state.

clue.text: One at the Met involved in improper arrest

indicators.note: involved in means the letters are enclosed within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone at the Metropolitan Police is caught up in a wrongful arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met reads as the London police; it is the Metropolitan Opera in New York.
explanation.definitionFit: The Met is New York's Metropolitan Opera, where one opera is a single work performed.

clue.text: One's not the lead in another scam

parts.note: a second is another one
a fiddle is a swindle or scam

explanation.surface: A con artist is not the ringleader in a further swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To play second fiddle is to take a subordinate role rather than lead.
